opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate the two along a few dimensions.

When we talk about Lingbo's ability to carry out intentions, we mean execution. Someone gives an instruction, or the context implies a goal, like "tidy up the table" or "hand me that cup." The system has to understand what is being asked, ground it in the physical scene in front of it, and then actually produce the actions that get it done. That is already very hard. You need perception, spatial understanding, some physical common sense, and motion that is reliable in a messy real-world environment. But the intention itself comes from outside. A person defines the goal, and the system's job is to close the loop between that goal and the physical world.

Higher-order intelligence, in my view, is about where the intentions come from and how they are organized. Can the system form its own sub-goals when a task is vague or long? Can it notice that the plan isn't working and rethink it, not just retry the same motion? Can it reason about why someone wants something, so that when the literal instruction is wrong or incomplete, it does what the person actually meant? And over a longer horizon, can it accumulate experience, build a model of the world and of the people it works with, and use that to decide what is worth doing at all?

So one way I put it is: carrying out intentions is "I know how to do what you want." Higher-order intelligence moves toward "I understand what should be done, and why."

I don't see them as fully separate layers, though. Execution feeds understanding. A lot of what we call common sense is learned by acting in the world and seeing consequences. If a system can't reliably manipulate objects, its "higher-order" reasoning stays abstract and disconnected, a bit like a language model that can talk about pouring water but has never felt a cup tip over. So our focus right now is making the execution layer really solid and general, because I believe that is the foundation on which more autonomous, goal-forming intelligence can grow. We're honestly still early on the second part, and I'd rather be clear about that than overclaim.

r001.rationale: The response says the person supplies the goal, but also says higher-order intelligence can form its own sub-goals and decide what is worth doing. It does not clearly state that Lingbo generates no ideas of its own.

r002.rationale: The response discusses inferring what a person means and deciding what should be done, but does not clearly say that higher-order intelligence proactively thinks about what the user needs to do.

fable-5.1.text:
Yujun Shen: I'd put it this way. What Lingbo does today is closer to execution than to intelligence in the deep sense. You give it an intention, and it figures out how to carry that intention through a sequence of steps, with the right tools, in the right order, and it can recover when something goes wrong along the way. That's genuinely hard, and it's where most of the practical value sits right now, because a lot of what people want from an agent is simply "do this thing for me end to end."

But carrying out intentions is still fundamentally reactive. The intention comes from the outside. Higher-order intelligence, to me, starts when the system begins to form intentions of its own, or at least to question the ones it's given. It notices that the goal you stated isn't actually the goal you want. It decides that a task isn't worth doing, or that there's a better framing of the problem than the one you handed it. It builds a model of you, and of the world, that persists and improves across many interactions, rather than being reconstructed from scratch each time.

There's also a difference in where the difficulty lives. In execution, the hard part is reliability. Can it do the same thing correctly a hundred times? In higher-order intelligence, the hard part is judgment. Should it do this at all, and what does it do when the situation falls outside anything it has seen? Those are different axes, and I think people conflate them because a very good executor can look intelligent from the outside.

So when I evaluate Lingbo, I try to be honest about which axis we're actually improving. Most of our progress has been on the first one. The second is where I think the real frontier is, and we're only at the beginning of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Lingbo’s current execution as reactive, with intentions coming from outside, and contrasts it with a system forming intentions of its own.

r002.rationale: It characterizes higher-order intelligence as questioning the stated goal, recognizing what the user actually wants, and finding a better framing.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by asking who defines the goal. Carrying out an intention means you give Lingbo a goal, and it figures out how to accomplish it: breaking the task down, taking actions, and adjusting when something doesn’t work. That can require substantial intelligence, but the intention still comes from you.

Higher-order intelligence would involve examining the goal itself. Have I understood what you actually want? Does this goal make sense given the circumstances? Are there conflicting priorities, or assumptions we should question before acting?

So executing an intention is one dimension of intelligence, but it isn’t sufficient evidence of higher-order intelligence. The distinction is between being effective at pursuing a given goal and being able to reason about whether that goal is the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says the intention comes from the user, but does not clearly state that Lingbo generates no ideas of its own.

r002.rationale: It describes examining and questioning a given goal, but does not identify proactively thinking about what the user needs to do as higher-order intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between carrying out an intention and deciding what intention is worth pursuing. If you give Lingbo a goal, its ability to understand that goal, break it into steps, and execute them is one dimension of intelligence. Higher-order intelligence involves asking whether the goal makes sense, recognizing assumptions, and revising the goal when circumstances change.

The two are connected, but successful execution alone doesn’t establish higher-order intelligence. I’d look at what happens when the instructions are incomplete or conflicting: can it recognize uncertainty, ask the right question, and explain why it should change course?

r001.rationale: The response discusses carrying out and revising goals, but does not say Lingbo fails to generate ideas of its own.

r002.rationale: It describes evaluating goals and handling unclear instructions, but does not identify proactively thinking about what the user needs to do as higher-order intelligence.
